samples.title: Cloud Computing and Azure Global Infrastructure
samples.definition: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, networking and software over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's public cloud: a global network of datacentres grouped into regions, on which you create resources through a single management layer instead of buying and racking your own hardware.
objectives: Explain cloud computing and the CapEx-to-OpEx shift in plain terms.
Compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and apply the shared responsibility model.
Describe Azure geographies, regions, region pairs and availability zones.
Choose a region using latency, compliance, service availability and price.
Answer the opening questions of an Azure administrator interview with confidence.

interview.question: What is the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS? Give an Azure example of each.
interview.answer: IaaS provides virtual infrastructure where you manage the OS and above, for example Azure Virtual Machines. PaaS provides a managed platform where you deploy code and data, for example Azure App Service or Azure SQL Database. SaaS is complete software you consume, for example Microsoft 365.
interview.explanation: A strong answer ties each model to who patches the operating system, which shows you understand the operational consequence, not just the acronym.

interview.question: Explain the shared responsibility model.
interview.answer: Security duties are split between the cloud provider and the customer. Microsoft always secures the physical datacentre, hosts and network. The customer always owns data, devices and identities. Responsibility for the OS, network controls and applications shifts towards Microsoft as you move from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS.
interview.explanation: Mention the 'always customer' items explicitly; many candidates wrongly say SaaS makes Microsoft responsible for everything.

interview.question: What is the difference between a region, an availability zone and a region pair?
interview.answer: A region is a geographic area containing one or more datacentres. An availability zone is a physically separate datacentre group inside a region with independent power, cooling and network. A region pair links two regions in the same geography for disaster recovery, staggered updates and prioritised recovery.
interview.explanation: Link each to the failure it protects against: zone for a datacentre failure, pair for a regional disaster.

interview.question: How would you choose an Azure region for a new workload?
interview.answer: First confirm compliance and data-residency requirements, then pick the region with the lowest latency to users that offers the required services, VM sizes and availability zones, and finally compare price between the shortlisted regions.
interview.explanation: Ordering the factors shows judgement; compliance is a hard constraint while price is a trade-off.

interview.question: What is the difference between scalability and elasticity?
interview.answer: Scalability is the ability to add capacity, either vertically (a bigger VM) or horizontally (more instances). Elasticity is scaling automatically in both directions in response to demand, such as autoscale rules on a scale set.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like the vertical versus horizontal distinction and a concrete Azure feature for elasticity.

example.title: Listing regions and zone support with Azure CLI
example.body: Before choosing where to deploy, an administrator checks which regions exist and which VM sizes support zones in a region. The CLI queries Azure Resource Manager, so the answer reflects your subscription's actual access.

code.source:
# All regions available to the subscription
az account list-locations --query "[].{name:name, display:displayName, pair:metadata.pairedRegion[0].name}" -o table

# Which zones a VM size supports in Central India
az vm list-skus --location centralindia --size Standard_D2s_v5 --zone -o table

practice.title: Shared responsibility lookup
practice.statement: Read a service model (IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, case-insensitive) and a list of responsibility layers. For each layer print who is responsible: Customer, Microsoft or Shared. Use this model: data, devices and accounts are always Customer; physical is always Microsoft; os is Customer for IaaS and Microsoft otherwise; applications and network are Customer for IaaS, Shared for PaaS and Microsoft for SaaS; identity is Customer for IaaS and Shared for PaaS and SaaS. Any other layer name prints Unknown. If the model itself is not one of the three, print only 'Invalid model'.
practice.objective: Encode the Azure shared responsibility model and use it to answer 'who owns this?' questions for any service model.

takeaways: Cloud turns up-front CapEx into consumption-based OpEx and adds elasticity.
IaaS gives most control and most responsibility; SaaS gives the least of both.
Data, devices and identities are always the customer's responsibility.
Availability zones protect against datacentre failure; region pairs protect against regional disasters.
Pick regions by compliance, latency, service availability and price, in that order.
Not every VM size or service exists in every region.

samples.title: Azure Resource Manager: Management Groups, Subscriptions and Resource Groups
samples.definition: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service for Azure: every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs or templates is authenticated, authorised and then sent by ARM to the right resource provider. ARM organises resources in a hierarchy of management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources, and access control, policy and budgets applied at one level are inherited by everything beneath it.
objectives: Explain what Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is and why every tool goes through it.
Describe the four-level hierarchy: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources.
Decide when to create a new subscription versus a new resource group.
Create and organise resource groups with Azure CLI and PowerShell.
Explain how settings applied at a higher scope are inherited by lower scopes.

interview.question: What is Azure Resource Manager?
interview.answer: ARM is Azure's management layer. All requests from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs and templates go through it; it authenticates the caller, checks RBAC and policy and forwards the request to the resource provider.
interview.explanation: Mention that this is why behaviour is consistent across tools and why templates can be declarative.

interview.question: When would you create a new subscription instead of a new resource group?
interview.answer: When you need a separate billing boundary, a strong access or environment boundary such as production versus development, separate quotas, or when an existing subscription is reaching scale limits. Resource groups are for grouping resources with the same lifecycle within a subscription.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want the boundary concept: subscriptions separate billing, access and quota; resource groups separate lifecycle.

interview.question: Can a resource group contain resources from different regions?
interview.answer: Yes. The resource group's location only stores its metadata. Resources inside can be in any region, although keeping metadata in a compliant region matters for some regulations.
interview.explanation: A common trick question. Mention the metadata point and the compliance nuance.

interview.question: What are management groups and why use them?
interview.answer: Management groups are containers above subscriptions. Policies and role assignments applied to a management group are inherited by all subscriptions beneath it, so governance is applied once for many subscriptions. They support up to six levels of depth under the Tenant Root Group.
interview.explanation: A strong answer gives an example structure (Platform, Landing Zones, Sandbox) and mentions inheritance.

interview.question: What happens when you move a resource to another resource group or subscription?
interview.answer: Both source and target groups are locked for writes during the move, and the resource gets a new resource ID. Not all resource types support moving, some have dependencies that must move together, and RBAC assignments made directly on the resource do not move with it.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the ID change and the need to update scripts, alerts and role assignments shows real operational experience.

example.title: Building a small hierarchy with Azure CLI
example.body: A governance team creates a management group for production, moves a subscription into it and creates a resource group for a web application. The resource group metadata lives in Central India.

code.source:
az account management-group create --name mg-prod --display-name "Production"
az account management-group subscription add --name mg-prod --subscription "Contoso-Prod"

az account set --subscription "Contoso-Prod"
az group create --name rg-shop-prod-cin --location centralindia --tags env=prod app=shop
az group list --query "[].{name:name, location:location}" -o table

practice.title: Resolve a scope path in the hierarchy
practice.statement: You are given parent links in an Azure hierarchy. Each line 'child parent' says that child is directly under parent; the top of the tree is the name 'root' (the Tenant Root Group). For each query, print the full path from root to the queried scope joined by ' > ', followed by its depth (number of links from root) in the form ' [depth d]'. If the queried name is not in the hierarchy (and is not 'root'), print '<name>: not found'.
practice.objective: Model the ARM hierarchy as parent links and print the inheritance path for any scope.

takeaways: Every Azure tool talks to Azure Resource Manager, which authenticates, authorises and applies policy.
Hierarchy: management groups > subscriptions > resource groups > resources.
Management groups support six levels of depth below the Tenant Root Group.
A subscription is a billing, quota and access boundary trusted by one Entra tenant.
Resource groups group by lifecycle; their location stores metadata only.
Assignments at a higher scope are inherited by every lower scope.

samples.title: Tags and Resource Locks for Organising and Protecting Resources
samples.definition: Tags are name-value pairs attached to Azure resources, resource groups and subscriptions to add metadata such as cost centre, environment or owner. Resource locks are management-plane safeguards that prevent accidental deletion (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly) to a scope and everything beneath it, regardless of the user's RBAC role.
objectives: Design a tagging strategy for cost reporting, ownership and automation.
Explain why tags are not inherited and how to enforce or inherit them with Azure Policy.
Compare CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks and predict which operations each blocks.
Explain lock inheritance and who is allowed to create or remove locks.
Recognise the side effects of ReadOnly locks on real services.

interview.question: What are tags used for in Azure?
interview.answer: Tags are name-value pairs that add metadata to resources, resource groups and subscriptions. They are used to group costs, identify owners and environments, and drive automation and policy.
interview.explanation: Give a concrete tag set (env, owner, costCenter) and a use such as cost reports grouped by tag.

interview.question: If you tag a resource group, do the resources inside get the tag?
interview.answer: No. Tags are not inherited. To get that behaviour you assign an Azure Policy such as 'Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing', which uses the Modify effect, and run a remediation task for existing resources.
interview.explanation: This is one of the most frequently asked AZ-104 points. Naming the Modify effect and remediation earns extra credit.

interview.question: What is the difference between CanNotDelete and ReadOnly locks?
interview.answer: CanNotDelete lets authorised users read and modify a resource but not delete it. ReadOnly lets them only read it; both modification and deletion are blocked.
interview.explanation: Add that locks inherit downward and that the most restrictive lock applies.

interview.question: An Owner cannot delete a resource. RBAC looks correct. What would you check?
interview.answer: Check for a resource lock on the resource, its resource group or the subscription, because locks override RBAC. Also check for deny assignments, for example from a managed application or a deployment stack.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like candidates who think beyond RBAC: locks and deny assignments both block Owners.

interview.question: Why might a ReadOnly lock on a storage account break an application or the portal?
interview.answer: Listing account keys is a POST operation on the management plane, which ReadOnly blocks. Tools and portal blades that need the keys fail, even though no data is being changed.
interview.explanation: This shows you know locks act on management operations and that 'read' in the portal is not always a GET.

example.title: Tagging a resource group and locking production
example.body: An administrator merges tags onto an existing resource group without removing other tags, then protects the group from deletion. The lock applies to every resource inside the group.

code.source:
# Merge tags (keeps existing tags)
az tag update --resource-id $(az group show -n rg-shop-prod-cin --query id -o tsv) \
  --operation Merge --tags costCenter=CC-104 owner=ops@contoso.in

# Prevent deletion of the whole resource group
az lock create --name lock-no-delete --lock-type CanNotDelete \
  --resource-group rg-shop-prod-cin --notes "Production - raise a change request"

az lock list --resource-group rg-shop-prod-cin -o table

practice.title: Evaluate resource locks for an operation
practice.statement: Scopes are written as slash-separated paths, for example 'sub1/rg-web/vm1'. A lock on a scope applies to that scope and every path beneath it (whole segments only: a lock on 'sub1/rg' does not apply to 'sub1/rg-web'). Lock types are CanNotDelete (blocks delete) and ReadOnly (blocks write and delete). Reads are never blocked. For each operation, find all locks that apply; if any of them blocks the operation, print 'BLOCKED by <type> at <scope>' choosing ReadOnly before CanNotDelete and, among locks of the same type, the one closest to the top (fewest segments). Otherwise print 'ALLOWED'.
practice.objective: Simulate how Azure combines inherited locks and decides whether a read, write or delete is allowed.

takeaways: Tags are name-value metadata used for cost, ownership and automation.
Tags are not inherited; use Azure Policy (Deny or Modify) to require or inherit them.
CanNotDelete allows modify but blocks delete; ReadOnly blocks modify and delete.
Locks are inherited by child scopes and override RBAC, even for Owners.
Only roles with Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* (Owner, User Access Administrator) manage locks.
ReadOnly locks can break operations that use POST, such as listing storage keys.

samples.title: Azure Management Tools: Portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and PowerShell
samples.definition: Azure offers several front ends to the same Azure Resource Manager API: the web-based Azure portal, the cross-platform Azure CLI (az commands), the Azure PowerShell Az module (Verb-AzNoun cmdlets) and Azure Cloud Shell, a browser-based shell with both tools pre-installed and already signed in. Because they all call ARM, anything created with one can be managed with another.
objectives: Compare the Azure portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell and know when to use each.
Translate common tasks between az commands and Az PowerShell cmdlets.
Filter and format CLI output with --query (JMESPath) and --output.
Explain how Cloud Shell authenticates and persists files.
Write a small, repeatable script instead of clicking through the portal.

interview.question: What tools can you use to manage Azure resources?
interview.answer: The Azure portal, Azure CLI, Azure PowerShell, Cloud Shell, REST APIs and SDKs, and infrastructure-as-code tools such as ARM templates, Bicep and Terraform. All of them go through Azure Resource Manager.
interview.explanation: Mentioning that they share ARM shows you understand why they are interchangeable.

interview.question: When would you prefer Azure CLI or PowerShell over the portal?
interview.answer: For repeatable, bulk or scheduled tasks, for anything that should be reviewed and version-controlled, and in pipelines. The portal is better for exploration and one-off checks.
interview.explanation: Interviewers look for an automation mindset; give a real example such as stopping all dev VMs nightly.

interview.question: How does Cloud Shell store files between sessions?
interview.answer: If you choose persistent storage, Cloud Shell mounts an Azure Files share from a storage account in your subscription as your home drive, so scripts and files survive. Ephemeral sessions keep nothing after they end.
interview.explanation: Knowing that storage is an Azure file share you pay for, and that sessions time out, shows hands-on use.

interview.question: How do you filter Azure CLI output to show only the names of running VMs?
interview.answer: Use 'az vm list -d' with a JMESPath query such as --query "[?powerState=='VM running'].name" and -o tsv or -o table.
interview.explanation: The -d (show details) flag is needed for powerState; mentioning it signals real experience.

interview.question: What is the key difference in how CLI and PowerShell return results?
interview.answer: Azure CLI returns text, JSON by default, which you shape with --query and parse in scripts. Azure PowerShell returns .NET objects whose properties can be filtered and selected directly in the pipeline.
interview.explanation: This explains why teams choose one or the other and why mixing them in one script is awkward.

example.title: The same task in CLI and PowerShell
example.body: Create a resource group and list running VMs in it. Notice that CLI filters JSON with JMESPath while PowerShell filters objects in the pipeline.

code.source:
# Azure CLI
az group create -n rg-lab-dev -l centralindia
az vm list -g rg-lab-dev -d --query "[?powerState=='VM running'].{name:name,size:hardwareProfile.vmSize}" -o table

# Azure PowerShell
New-AzResourceGroup -Name rg-lab-dev -Location centralindia
Get-AzVM -ResourceGroupName rg-lab-dev -Status |
  Where-Object PowerState -eq 'VM running' |
  Select-Object Name, @{n='Size';e={$_.HardwareProfile.VmSize}}

practice.title: Script a reusable lab environment
practice.statement: Your trainer creates the same lab for every batch: a resource group rg-az104-lab in Central India tagged env=lab and owner=<your email>, a general-purpose v2 storage account with locally redundant storage, and a CanNotDelete lock on the group. Write an Azure CLI script that builds it, a query that proves it exists, and the PowerShell equivalent of the resource group and lock steps. Finally, write the single command that removes everything at the end of the batch and explain why it fails until the lock is removed.
practice.objective: Replace a sequence of portal clicks with a repeatable script and its PowerShell equivalent.

takeaways: Portal, CLI, PowerShell and Cloud Shell all call the same Azure Resource Manager API.
Azure CLI uses az <group> <action>; filter with --query (JMESPath) and format with -o.
Az PowerShell uses Verb-AzNoun cmdlets and returns objects you can pipe.
Cloud Shell is pre-authenticated, browser-based and can persist files on an Azure file share.
Use scripts or Bicep for anything you need to repeat; use the portal to explore.

firstLesson.title: Cloud Computing and Azure Global Infrastructure
objectives: Explain cloud computing and the CapEx-to-OpEx shift in plain terms.
Compare IaaS, PaaS and SaaS and apply the shared responsibility model.
Describe Azure geographies, regions, region pairs and availability zones.
Choose a region using latency, compliance, service availability and price.
Answer the opening questions of an Azure administrator interview with confidence.
firstLesson.definition: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, networking and software over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's public cloud: a global network of datacentres grouped into regions, on which you create resources through a single management layer instead of buying and racking your own hardware.

theory.heading: Why organisations move to the cloud
theory.body: On-premises IT requires large up-front capital expenditure (CapEx) on servers, storage and datacentre space that must be sized for peak demand and then sits idle most of the time. The cloud converts this into operational expenditure (OpEx): you pay for what you consume, scale up for a festival sale and scale back down the next day. Administrators care about this because it changes their job from replacing failed disks to designing for elasticity, governance and cost control.
points: High availability: services are designed to keep running despite component failures.
Scalability and elasticity: add or remove capacity manually (scale) or automatically (elastic).
Agility: provision a VM or database in minutes, not weeks.
Global reach: deploy close to users in many countries.
Consumption-based pricing: no idle hardware bill, but you must watch for waste.

theory.heading: Service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
theory.body: The service model decides how much of the stack you manage. In IaaS (Azure Virtual Machines) you manage the operating system, patching, runtime and application while Microsoft manages the physical host. In PaaS (App Service, Azure SQL Database) Microsoft also manages the OS and runtime, so you focus on code, configuration and data. In SaaS (Microsoft 365) you only consume the application and manage your data, users and devices.
points: IaaS: most control, most responsibility (VMs, managed disks, virtual networks).
PaaS: platform handles OS patching and scaling plumbing (App Service, Azure SQL, Functions).
SaaS: finished software delivered over the internet (Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365).
Serverless (Functions, Logic Apps) is a PaaS style billed per execution.

theory.heading: The shared responsibility model
theory.body: Security and operations are split between Microsoft and the customer. Microsoft always owns physical datacentres, hosts and the physical network. The customer always owns their data, endpoints (devices) and accounts and identities, in every model. Everything in between moves from the customer towards Microsoft as you go from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS. This is why a breached password is always the customer's problem, even on SaaS.
points: Always customer: information and data, devices, accounts and identities.
Always Microsoft: physical hosts, physical network, physical datacentre.
Operating system: customer in IaaS, Microsoft in PaaS and SaaS.
Applications and network controls: customer in IaaS, shared in PaaS, Microsoft in SaaS.
Identity and directory infrastructure: customer in IaaS, shared in PaaS and SaaS.

theory.heading: Azure global infrastructure
theory.body: A region is a set of datacentres within a latency-defined perimeter, such as Central India (Pune) or South India (Chennai). Regions are grouped into geographies that respect data-residency and compliance boundaries. Many regions have a paired region in the same geography; Azure staggers platform updates across pairs and prioritises recovery of one region in each pair during a wide outage. Availability zones are physically separate datacentres (independent power, cooling and networking) inside one region, normally three per supported region.
points: Region: where your resource physically runs; choose it per resource.
Availability zone: protects against a datacentre failure inside a region.
Region pair: protects against a whole-region disaster; used by GRS storage replication.
Sovereign clouds (Azure Government, Azure operated by 21Vianet in China) are isolated instances.
Not every service or VM size is available in every region; check before designing.

theory.heading: Choosing a region
theory.body: Interviewers often ask how you would pick a region. A strong answer weighs four factors in order: compliance and data residency (Indian banking data may need to stay in India), latency to users, availability of the required services and zones, and price, which varies between regions for the same VM size.
points: Compliance first: some data must not leave the country.
Latency: put workloads near users; test with tools such as Azure speed tests.
Capability: zones, specific VM series or services may be missing in smaller regions.
Cost: the same SKU can cost noticeably more in one region than another.

example.title: Listing regions and zone support with Azure CLI
example.body: Before choosing where to deploy, an administrator checks which regions exist and which VM sizes support zones in a region. The CLI queries Azure Resource Manager, so the answer reflects your subscription's actual access.

code.source:
# All regions available to the subscription
az account list-locations --query "[].{name:name, display:displayName, pair:metadata.pairedRegion[0].name}" -o table

# Which zones a VM size supports in Central India
az vm list-skus --location centralindia --size Standard_D2s_v5 --zone -o table

use_cases.title: Seasonal retail
use_cases.description: An e-commerce site scales out web servers for a sale weekend and scales back in afterwards, paying only for the extra hours.

use_cases.title: Data residency
use_cases.description: An Indian fintech keeps customer data in Central India with disaster recovery in South India to satisfy regulator guidance.

use_cases.title: Datacentre exit
use_cases.description: A company lifts and shifts ageing servers to Azure VMs (IaaS) before modernising to App Service (PaaS).

use_cases.title: Global SaaS
use_cases.description: A start-up serves customers in India, Europe and the US by deploying the same template to three regions.

demonstration.description: Map common tasks to the party responsible under each service model. This is the reasoning interviewers want when they ask 'who patches the OS on App Service?'.

code.source:
Task                         IaaS (VM)   PaaS (App Service)   SaaS (Microsoft 365)
Patch the guest OS           Customer    Microsoft            Microsoft
Configure app network rules  Customer    Shared               Microsoft
Protect user passwords       Customer    Customer             Customer
Replace a failed disk        Microsoft   Microsoft            Microsoft

demonstration.output: Data, devices and identities stay with the customer in every model; physical infrastructure stays with Microsoft; the OS moves to Microsoft as soon as you use PaaS.

takeaways: Cloud turns up-front CapEx into consumption-based OpEx and adds elasticity.
IaaS gives most control and most responsibility; SaaS gives the least of both.
Data, devices and identities are always the customer's responsibility.
Availability zones protect against datacentre failure; region pairs protect against regional disasters.
Pick regions by compliance, latency, service availability and price, in that order.
Not every VM size or service exists in every region.

practice.title: Shared responsibility lookup
practice.objective: Encode the Azure shared responsibility model and use it to answer 'who owns this?' questions for any service model.
practice.statement: Read a service model (IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, case-insensitive) and a list of responsibility layers. For each layer print who is responsible: Customer, Microsoft or Shared. Use this model: data, devices and accounts are always Customer; physical is always Microsoft; os is Customer for IaaS and Microsoft otherwise; applications and network are Customer for IaaS, Shared for PaaS and Microsoft for SaaS; identity is Customer for IaaS and Shared for PaaS and SaaS. Any other layer name prints Unknown. If the model itself is not one of the three, print only 'Invalid model'.
practice.input_format: Line 1: the service model. Line 2: N, the number of layers. Next N lines: one layer name each (case-insensitive).
practice.output_format: For each layer, one line '<layer>: <owner>' with the layer in lowercase, or a single line 'Invalid model'.

example.output:
os: Microsoft
data: Customer
network: Shared

constraints: Layer names are compared in lowercase.
practice.starter:
model = input().strip().lower()
n = int(input())
layers = [input().strip().lower() for _ in range(n)]

# TODO: build a table of layer -> (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) owners and print each answer
practice.solution:
TABLE = {
    'data': ('Customer', 'Customer', 'Customer'),
    'devices': ('Customer', 'Customer', 'Customer'),
    'accounts': ('Customer', 'Customer', 'Customer'),
    'identity': ('Customer', 'Shared', 'Shared'),
    'applications': ('Customer', 'Shared', 'Microsoft'),
    'network': ('Customer', 'Shared', 'Microsoft'),
    'os': ('Customer', 'Microsoft', 'Microsoft'),
    'physical': ('Microsoft', 'Microsoft', 'Microsoft'),
}
MODELS = {'iaas': 0, 'paas': 1, 'saas': 2}

model = input().strip().lower()
n = int(input())
layers = [input().strip().lower() for _ in range(n)]

if model not in MODELS:
    print('Invalid model')
else:
    col = MODELS[model]
    for layer in layers:
        owner = TABLE[layer][col] if layer in TABLE else 'Unknown'
        print(f'{layer}: {owner}')
explanation: Store the model as a dictionary from layer to a tuple of owners for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
Map the service model to a column index; reject anything else with 'Invalid model'.
For each layer, look up the owner in the chosen column, falling back to 'Unknown'.
Notice that the 'always customer' rows never change: that is the key interview point.

tests.output:
os: Microsoft
data: Customer
network: Shared

os: Customer
physical: Microsoft
identity: Customer
applications: Customer

tests.input:
SAAS
5
accounts
network
identity
devices
billing
tests.output:
accounts: Customer
network: Microsoft
identity: Shared
devices: Customer
billing: Unknown

quiz.question: Under the shared responsibility model, which item remains the customer's responsibility even for a SaaS application such as Microsoft 365?
quiz.explanation: Accounts and identities, data and devices are always the customer's responsibility. Infrastructure and, in SaaS, the application are Microsoft's.

quiz.question: Your company wants its web application to survive the failure of a single datacentre in Central India without moving to another region. What should you use?
quiz.explanation: Availability zones are physically separate datacentres within one region, so a zone-redundant deployment survives a single datacentre failure.

quiz.question: Which Azure service is an example of Platform as a Service (PaaS)?
quiz.explanation: App Service runs your code on a platform where Microsoft manages the OS and runtime. VMs and Dedicated Host are IaaS; Microsoft 365 is SaaS.

quiz.question: A bank must keep customer data inside India and wants the lowest latency for users in Mumbai. Which factor must be satisfied before comparing prices between regions?
options: Whether the region has the newest VM series
The size of the region's datacentres
quiz.explanation: Compliance and residency are hard constraints. Only regions that satisfy them should then be compared on latency, capability and price.

quiz.question: What is a benefit of Azure region pairs?
options: They remove the need for backups
They make every resource zone-redundant automatically
They share a single IP address space
Planned platform updates are rolled out to one region of the pair at a time
quiz.explanation: Azure staggers planned updates across the two regions of a pair and prioritises recovering one region of each pair in a widespread outage.
